hints: Count horizontal divisions for one complete sine wave on the c.r.o. screen, from the same point on successive waves, using the $5.0 \text{ ms/div}$ time-base.
Measure over more than one cycle where possible, for example two full waves span about $5.6$ divisions, then divide to get divisions per period.
Convert divisions per period to period $T$ in seconds, then use $f = 1/T$ and check the unit $\text{Hz}$.
walkthrough: Note the horizontal axis is time. Time-base $5.0 \text{ ms/div}$ means each horizontal division equals $5.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}$.
Find the period by counting divisions for one cycle. One full sine wave occupies about $2.8$ divisions. Measuring two cycles over about $5.6$ divisions gives the same result.
Calculate the period: $T = 2.8 \times 5.0 \text{ ms} = 14 \text{ ms} = 14 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}$.
Calculate frequency from $f = 1/T$: $f = 1/(14 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}) \approx 71 \text{ s}^{-1} = 71 \text{ Hz}$.

options.A: Too low. This would need a period of about $17.5 \text{ ms}$, which is about $3.5$ divisions, longer than one wave on the trace.
options.B: One period is about $2.8$ divisions, so $T \approx 14 \text{ ms}$ and $f = 1/T \approx 71 \text{ Hz}$.
options.C: Too high by almost a factor of two. This comes from using about $1.75$ divisions as the period instead of the full $2.8$ divisions.
options.D: Too high by a factor of two. This comes from mistaking half a cycle for a full period, giving $T \approx 7.0 \text{ ms}$.
